source: Papafragou, Hulbert & Trueswell (2008) Does language guide event perception? Evidence from eye movements
finding: Greek and English speakers looked at different parts of a motion scene while preparing to speak, but not while just memorising it.
numbers: N=17 English + 17 Greek, 12 clip-art motion events, 3 s videos. Bounded events: English used manner verbs in 72% of descriptions vs Greek 36%; unbounded 76% vs 54%. Median speech onset 1267 ms. Linguistic task first-look Language x Path/Manner: F1(1,16)=5.50, p=.03, partial eta2=.26; by items F2(1,11)=3.61, p=.08 (marginal). No such interaction in the nonlinguistic task. Total looking time to path vs manner did not interact with Language in either task.
quote: when freely inspecting ongoing events, as in the memorization task, people allocated attention similarly regardless of the language they speak
limits: Small N. The key interaction is only significant by subjects and marginal by items. Only motion verbs, only English vs Greek.
agent_relevance: Language-specific encoding bites only when the task is to produce language. If the agent is not producing text in a given format, that format's habits should not steer how it reads the input.

source: Papafragou, Hulbert & Trueswell (2008) Does language guide event perception? Evidence from eye movements
finding: The language effect is about timing and order of attention, not about what is attended overall. Greek speakers looked first to the path endpoint, then to manner; English speakers looked to manner first and then the endpoint.
numbers: Both groups looked more at the path endpoint than at manner overall in both tasks (linguistic F1(1,16)=19.71, partial eta2=.55; nonlinguistic F1(1,14)=28.45, partial eta2=.67). Differences appeared within the first second of motion onset, with a reversal after about 1.5 s.
limits: Time-course reading is largely descriptive in the 2008 paper.
agent_relevance: The effect is a re-ordering of subtasks during planning. For an agent this resembles a plan-then-write step shaped by the output format.

source: Papafragou, Hulbert & Trueswell (2008) Does language guide event perception? Evidence from eye movements
finding: Authors state that language-specific preferences for event encoding do not intrude into ordinary event perception when no speech is needed. This discriminates the weak thinking-for-speaking view from the strong Whorfian view.
numbers: Nonlinguistic condition: N=15-17 per group; path-first bias in both groups (F1(1,14)=9.45, partial eta2=.40), no Language interaction. Differences arose only after motion stopped: people studied aspects their language does not routinely encode in verbs.
quote: effects of language arise only when linguistic forms are recruited to achieve the task
limits: One task family (motion). A null with about 16 per group is weak evidence of no effect.
agent_relevance: Supports scoping language effects to the production stage, not to how the agent reads evidence already given.

source: Papafragou, Massey & Gleitman (2002, 2006) motion encoding vs memory/categorisation, Greek and English
finding: Earlier work from the same group found no cross-language difference in memory or categorisation of path and manner for Greek vs English, and for Spanish vs English (Gennari et al. 2002).
numbers: Description only, from the introduction of Papafragou et al. (2008): production asymmetry present, no difference in classification or memory.
limits: Opened only as described in the 2008 paper; the 2002 and 2006 papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: Language differences in production do not automatically become differences in non-linguistic memory.

source: Gennari, Sloman, Malt & Fitch (2002) Motion events in language and cognition
finding: Spanish and English speakers described 36 motion events as expected (Spanish more path verbs) but did not differ in recognition memory, even after verbal encoding. A language effect appeared in similarity judgements only after verbal encoding.
numbers: 47 Spanish (Argentina) and 46 English (Brown) speakers across Naming First (16 En/15 Sp), Free Encoding (15 each) and Shadow (verbal interference; 16 each). Spanish path-verb proportion 0.80; manner expression 0.71. Manner expression English 0.86 in all conditions; Spanish 0.64 (Naming First), 0.76 (Free), 0.73 (Shadow).
quote: participants linguistically encoded the stimuli before giving responses to nonlinguistic tasks
limits: Different populations and settings per language. The similarity effect is explained by the authors as task-context use of linguistic regularities.
agent_relevance: Naming first can steer a later judgement. Writing a verbal description before deciding may import language-specific bias; free-form reasoning text may do the same to an agent's later decision.

source: Gennari, Sloman, Malt & Fitch (2002) Motion events in language and cognition
finding: Authors argue linguistic labels and non-linguistic event concepts are dissociable, and that language effects in earlier relativity work (e.g. Lucy 1993) may reflect task order.
numbers: Language bias in similarity reflected general lexical patterns (event-generic strategies), not the label given to a specific action.
limits: Argument by the authors; task order only tested through the non-linguistic-encoding condition.
agent_relevance: The order of describe-then-judge vs judge-then-describe matters for what gets carried forward.

source: Chen, Papafragou & Trueswell (2026) The Goal Bias Emerges During Motion Event Perception and Affects Language Production and Memory
finding: The Goal bias (more attention to the endpoint than the source of a motion event) is visible in eye movements during encoding, is larger in free inspection than during speech planning, and predicts whether the Source is later mentioned or remembered.
numbers: N=128 English speakers (27 excluded for track loss in eye analysis); 16 critical 5 s events. Mention rate Goal 97.7% vs Source 87.5% (beta=-1.048, p=.006). Memory change detection Linguistic: Goal 62.5%, Source 53.1%; Non-linguistic: Goal 50.9%, Source 42.9%. Fixation Goal 1312 ms vs Source 913 ms (beta=199.41, p<.001). Condition x AOI beta=-113.42, p<.001: speaking raised attention to Source. Cluster 1900-5000 ms, p<.001.
quote: we provide the first evidence that the Goal bias appears during visual encoding of motion events
limits: English only, so no cross-language test. The gaze-to-mention link is correlational. Heavy exclusion (27 of 128).
agent_relevance: Planning to speak redistributes attention to what must be mentioned. A scaffold step that lists every component (source and goal) before writing may counter the default endpoint bias.

source: Montero-Melis (2021) Consistency in Motion Event Encoding Across Languages
finding: Swedish speakers almost always use one syntactic frame for caused motion, while Spanish speakers vary a lot. Spanish variation comes mainly from the speaker, not from the event, which contradicts the event-properties account.
numbers: N=84 (42 Swedish, 42 Spanish), 32 caused-motion events. Swedish satellite-framed 97% of descriptions; Spanish verb-framed 59%, satellite 35%, no path 6%. Spanish speaker random-intercept SD 2.37 vs event SD 0.78 (more than 3x); slopes 1.10 vs 0.29.
limits: Two languages only. Production data, no non-linguistic task.
agent_relevance: Languages differ in how strongly they channel speakers into one schema. Output style may differ in how rigidly it fixes the encoding.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Under the Shadow of Babel: How Language Shapes Reasoning in LLMs
finding: LLM paper framed as linguistic relativity: models show language-typical attention patterns and rigid causal word-order preferences that lower accuracy on atypical inputs, especially in Chinese.
numbers: BICAUSE: aligned Chinese/English causal reasoning, forward and reversed forms, 8 domains. Table 1 accuracy En vs Zh: Llama-3.2-3B 27.0 vs 56.8; Mistral-7B 95.8 vs 88.5; Qwen1.5-72B 95.5 vs 92.2; Qwen1.5-1.8B 91.0 vs 91.2. Paraphrased (Table 2): Mistral-7B 93.8 vs 81.5; Qwen1.5-1.8B 88.5 vs 76.8; Qwen1.5-14B 97.5 vs 97.5.
limits: About 50 items per domain cell. Direction inconsistent across models (Llama-3.2-3B better in Chinese). Tests an output-language habit, not thinking-for-speaking; an analogy at most.
agent_relevance: The language a task is posed in changes accuracy by up to about 12 points on the same causal content for some models and by nothing for others. Test the scaffold in each prompt language we serve.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Under the Shadow of Babel: How Language Shapes Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Authors claim that when causal reasoning succeeds, model representations converge across languages.
numbers: Abstract finding (3): shared semantic abstractions across Chinese and English when reasoning is correct.
quote: model representations converge toward semantically aligned abstractions across languages
limits: Interpretation of internal analysis; not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Suggests a shared conceptual layer under language-specific surface forms, matching the human result that cognition is not rewritten by language.

source: Thierry (2016) Neurolinguistic Relativity: How Language Flexes Human Perception and Cognition
finding: Review arguing for mild language effects on perception and event conceptualisation. Cites eye-tracking (Flecken et al. 2015; Papafragou et al. 2008) as showing mild influence, and grammatical-aspect studies linking aspect to endpoint attention.
numbers: Narrative review; no pooled effect size. Non-aspect speakers (German, Swedish) mention the goal of an unfinished motion event more than aspect speakers (English, French).
limits: Written by an advocate group (Bangor lab). The neural claims rest on small ERP samples.
agent_relevance: Gives the pro-relativity side of the dispute; read alongside the null results.

source: Athanasopoulos et al. (2015) German-English bilinguals switch event construal with language
finding: Fluent German-English bilinguals shift between goal-oriented and motion-oriented construal depending on language context (as described by Thierry 2016).
numbers: No figures in the passage read.
limits: Not opened; secondhand via Thierry (2016).
agent_relevance: Language-context switching is a precedent for output-language toggles changing the frame.

source: von Stutterheim, Flecken, Carroll and colleagues (2012-2014) grammatical aspect and endpoint attention
finding: Speakers of languages without grammatical aspect (German, Swedish) mention the goal of an unfinished motion event more than speakers of aspect languages (English, French), with matching attention differences.
numbers: Cited via Thierry (2016) with Bylund & Athanasopoulos (2013, 2014); no figures read.
limits: Not opened; secondhand.
agent_relevance: The grammatical requirement of the output language steers which element is planned first.

source: Goller, Lee, Ansorge & Choi (2017) Effects of Language Background on Gaze Behavior: Korean vs German
finding: Korean and German speakers rated similarity of tight/loose containment and support videos along their own language's categories and looked at Figure and Ground differently, without speaking.
numbers: N=27 (df=25). Language x Pair F(3,75)=8.02, p=.001, partial eta2=.24. German rated tight-in/loose-in more similar than Korean (t(25)=3.31, d=1.27); Korean rated tight-in/tight-on more similar (t(25)=2.76, d=1.06). Korean looked equally long at Figure and Ground; German biased to Ground.
limits: Small N. Conflicts with the null of Papafragou 2008 for non-linguistic attention. Explicit similarity ratings may invite covert labelling.
agent_relevance: Counter-evidence to a pure production-stage account: categories can leak into silent tasks in the spatial-relations domain. Keep the weak claim for motion verbs only.

source: Event Segmentation in Language and Cognition (2026), English vs Turkish
finding: Large English vs Turkish study: linguistic event units differ strongly but non-linguistic event segmentation and enumeration do not.
numbers: N=39 English, 42 Turkish; 30 motion clips of 2500 ms. Experiment 1 description: Turkish speakers gave more multi-clause descriptions (beta=-3.84, SE=0.57, z=-6.67, p<.001). Experiments 2 and 3 (segmentation, enumeration) showed no matching language difference.
quote: conceptual and linguistic event units are related but distinct levels of event structure
limits: A null on non-linguistic tasks is absence of evidence at this N, though the sample is larger than earlier cross-linguistic segmentation work. English and Turkish only.
agent_relevance: Sentence units differ by language but event units do not. Plan on event units, not on sentence units.

source: Development of Event Segmentation in Language and Cognition (2026), Turkish children and adults
finding: Turkish 4-5 year olds and adults: linguistic units shift with age (adults and some 5-year-olds use more units for direction changes) but eye-tracked dwell times are the same across ages.
numbers: Abstract and partial text only. Linguistic task: systematic difference in adults, smaller in 5-year-olds, absent in 4-year-olds. Non-linguistic dwell time: similar profiles with and without direction changes.
limits: Exact test statistics not extracted.
agent_relevance: Language-specific encoding strengthens with learning while perception stays stable, which places the habit in the production routine.

source: Cross-Linguistic Coordination of Overt Attention and Speech Production (2026), English/Portuguese/Japanese
finding: Eye-tracking in English, Portuguese and Japanese: how similar the meanings of two descriptions are strongly predicts how similar the scan patterns are, even across languages. Syntax adds a secondary, short-lived effect in the early planning phase.
numbers: N=74 (24 English, 28 Portuguese, 20 Japanese). Semantic similarity predicted scan similarity in all three languages, across scenes and languages; syntactic similarity effect only within language and within scene, and only in planning.
limits: Cued-object scene description, not motion typology. Effect sizes not extracted from the text I read.
agent_relevance: A near-universal semantic layer drives where people look; syntax matters locally when linearising. Fits a scaffold where content selection is language-neutral and linearisation comes last.

source: Cognitive Representation of Spontaneous Motion in a Second Language: Chinese learners of English (2019)
finding: Chinese learners of English judged similarity of spontaneous motion in match-to-sample. Explicit choices favoured path matching in all groups; reaction times differed by background and L2 learners were slower even at advanced levels.
numbers: N=160 in 5 groups of 32 (English monolinguals, Chinese monolinguals, three English proficiency groups). Chinese monolinguals responded significantly faster than English monolinguals, especially for path matches; L2 learners slower than monolinguals at all proficiencies.
limits: Chinese monolingual group was vocational high-school students, not matched in age or education. Authors read it as weak relativity.
agent_relevance: Explicit choices show no language difference but speed does. Check implicit measures (latency, token behaviour), not only final answers.

source: Contrastive Verbal Guidance: A Beneficial Context for Attention To Events and Their Memory (2025)
finding: Verbal guidance before an action changes attention to action goals and later memory; a negated instruction guides as well as an assertive one for contrasting paths.
numbers: Experiment 1 N=35: assertive instructions raised overall recall; negating the later path for contrastive actions was equally facilitative. Experiment 2 varied instruction overlap with the action.
limits: Not cross-language; one language, small sample.
agent_relevance: Human evidence that instruction wording redirects attention at encoding. A prompt that names what to look for acts like verbal guidance.

source: Slobin (1996) From 'thought and language' to 'thinking for speaking'
finding: Origin claim: speakers attend to the dimensions of experience their language requires them to mark when preparing an utterance.
numbers: No numbers; theoretical paper, as summarised in Papafragou et al. (2008).
limits: Not opened; seen only through later papers.
agent_relevance: Defines the weak form usable here: the effect is local to encoding a message.

source: Gleitman, January, Nappa & Trueswell (2007) On the give and take between event apprehension and utterance formulation
finding: Cited by Papafragou et al. (2008) as showing that attention to a to-be-mentioned entity affects early utterance planning.
numbers: Not read; Europe PMC full text returned an error.
limits: Not opened. Competing account: structure chosen first vs attention shapes structure.
agent_relevance: Whether planning order drives output order.

source: Griffin & Bock (2000) What the eyes say about speaking
finding: Cited in the 2008 paper as showing rapid event apprehension before and during utterance formulation.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Background for a fast event-apprehension stage preceding linguistic encoding.

source: Gerwien & von Stutterheim (2018) cross-linguistic event description and segmentation
finding: Cited in the 2026 event-segmentation paper as an earlier cross-linguistic study with smaller samples.
numbers: Sample size not extracted.
limits: Not opened; secondhand.
agent_relevance: Context for replication adequacy.

source: Bylund & Athanasopoulos (2013-2014) aspect, endpoint and event construal
finding: Cited by Thierry (2016) for non-aspect-language speakers specifying goals more than aspect-language speakers.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened; secondhand.
agent_relevance: A second line of evidence not yet tested on models.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Under the Shadow of Babel: How Language Shapes Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Gap: my searches found no LLM paper that tests thinking-for-speaking or motion-event typology directly. The nearest is BICAUSE, an output-language bias study.
numbers: Four WebSearch calls on this topic found none; a fifth, for 'Do Llamas work in English?', was refused by the shared budget cap. arXiv API and OpenAlex gave empty or rate-limited results.
limits: Absence of evidence from a narrow search budget, not a systematic review.
agent_relevance: Treat our own test as new work: ask the agent to describe an event in a set format before answering and check whether format choices shift which entities it covers.
